speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Every injury or death to one of our Servicemen is an occasion marked by sadness and regret for the whole SAF family.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our SAF commanders know that the sons of families entrusted to them during National Service (NS) are precious.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Even as they are responsible to train them to raise and maintain a credible and decisive SAF to defend Singapore, our commanders are clear that they need to do this as safely as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our safety standards are among the highest for militaries globally and I am not talking just subjective assessments.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If you look at training injuries, training deaths and you compare them with similar militaries in a peacetime posture, our safety standards are credible.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: SAF will endeavour to do its utmost to train safely but, realistically speaking, all of us recognise that in military organisations, injuries and deaths can happen despite the best efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Each time an injury or death occurs, we must ensure that independent and impartial investigative processes are instituted to determine the key facts, arrive at appropriate conclusions, take the corrective measures to ensure that mistakes, if any, are not repeated.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This includes punishing those held responsible for reckless and negligent acts that have led to the death or injury.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Like civilians, SAF Servicemen can be charged and punished in the civilian criminal Courts even if the acts were committed in the course of duties but amount to criminal offences under general law.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The names are on public record for these two cases but I shall not repeat them today, so as not to resurrect painful memories for the families involved.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In 2011, a Lance Corporal was killed when a truck reversed into him.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The driver of the truck was charged in the criminal Courts for an offence of causing death by a negligent act under section 304 of the Penal Code.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: He was tried in Court and the Court fined him $3,000 – no detention.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Company Sergeant Major involved in that accident was not prosecuted by the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC).

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Attorney-General decided that there was insufficient evidence to prosecute him in the criminal Courts.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: SAF charged him under military law for failing to ensure that the Servicemen kept a safe distance away from the vehicle as the supervising officer.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: A second example: in 2012, an SAF vehicle overturned during an exercise, causing the death of a passenger.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Conducting Officer who appointed a Serviceman to drive the military vehicle even when he knew that the Serviceman did not have a driving licence, was convicted in the criminal Courts and sentenced to six months' imprisonment as he was found to have committed a rash act and attempted to pervert the course of justice.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is then up to the criminal Courts to determine the level of culpability and commensurate punishments.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: SAF fully accepts these judicial processes and, indeed, deems them necessary so that our SAF Servicemen are held accountable for their actions.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: All these processes were applied in the tragic death of the late Private (PTE) Lee Rui Feng Dominique Sarron.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In the case of PTE Lee, which the Member has asked about, Mdm Speaker, a Coroner's Inquiry was held in August 2013.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Coroner's Inquiry is an open hearing, accessible to the public and the media.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The family of the late PTE Lee and their legal counsel were also present and were given opportunities to address any questions that they might have relating to PTE Lee's death to the Court.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They were also allowed to pose questions to the two SAF officers involved during the hearing.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Coroner's full findings and conclusions are open for public viewing upon application and approval by the Court.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The family has a copy of the Coroner's full findings and conclusions.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In his findings, the Coroner also opined that it was clear that the deceased's allergic reaction was "unlikely to have been predicted", at paragraph 66 of the Coroner's findings.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: AGC informed the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) to consider taking disciplinary action against the Servicemen who had breached Training Safety Regulations (TSR).

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If there were sufficient grounds to deem the Servicemen criminally liable for PTE Lee's death, they would have been prosecuted in the criminal Courts, as the AGC had done in previous cases cited above.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They were also punished with penalties consistent with other Servicemen who have committed similar offences, through fines and delay in promotion.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Both officers have suffered a setback in their careers.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For MINDEF and SAF, when training incidents occur, we have to rely on our judicial system to determine the facts and mete out the appropriate punishment where required.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It would be wrong and unfair to punish SAF Servicemen beyond the level of offence committed which has been determined by independent and impartial judicial processes.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Allergy to zinc chloride from smoke grenades is known but rare, which is why till today, many militaries still use this type of smoke grenade, including the US military and the Republic of Korea.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In the SAF's own history, we have been using this type of smoke grenades.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Members of the House here who had done NS would have tested it.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have been using this type of smoke grenade for over 30 years and hundreds of thousands of soldiers have been exposed to it and this is our first and only case.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: While SAF has decided to do so, let me point out that there is no safety requirement internationally that precludes the use of such smoke grenades.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Indeed, other militaries, as I have said, continue to use it and this underscores the fact that allergy to zinc chloride is rare so that the militaries have chosen to continue their use and accept that risk.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The two SAF officers involved will carry with them the pain of this incident for the rest of their lives.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But I do not believe that they started that fateful day intending at all to harm the soldiers under their charge.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These are not the values of our SAF commanders.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As sad and tragic as this incident has been, we must do right for all involved.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I feel very sad for the family members of PTE Lee and I know that all Members here feel that.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Some of us have experienced losing a loved one and we can feel and empathise with the pain losing someone so young in his life.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We feel very sad for them for their great loss.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: My personal prayers go to the family for peace and comfort, even as they continue to deal with this difficult and tragic loss of a loved one.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister explain to the House, normally, after an officer has been convicted under military law, what would be the time period that he would be held back for promotion?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I can give a few examples for consideration: the waiver can be limited to actual operations and should not apply to training, or when a death or personal injury occurred as a result of omission from observing Training Safety Regulations (TSRs), or when negligence of an officer has some causal connection with the death or personal injury.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, it is quite self-evident that there are equivalents to determine the level of culpability, the severity of the offence and the delays in promotions and fines are commensurate.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I presume that in law, in the Courts, they have to stack it against a whole range of offences that makes sense as an overall system.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have tried to give one measure in which the delay in promotion amounted to half the annual salary.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Member has asked about the Proceedings Act.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That is something which, if the Member feels strongly about, he can put up a Motion to amend the Act.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The nub of the issue is this: how much protection should we give to our security forces when they are doing their job?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: A policeman chasing a potential suspect whom he thinks is going to commit harm, discharges a firearm, hits someone else.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If our military officer or military Servicemen who now make patrols in Changi Airport and Jurong Island, and if they see a significant threat, and they are tasked to protect that place or island, do they discharge the firearm?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Or will they hold back, thinking, "If I make a wrong decision, then, I am on my own." And there is a civil suit; not trivial.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Think about what happened at the Shangri-La Dialogue.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Twenty-eight defence ministers in that hotel; either defence ministers or deputy defence ministers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I went to Shangri-La Dialogue that year, early in the morning, 7.00 am, my car was diverted.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They were not sure of the facts, possible bomb explosion because despite all the concrete barricades, a car had attempted to rush through the concrete barricade.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: What do you do if you were in charge; if you are meant to secure the place?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You think, "Well, I am not protected if I make a mistake." Our Home Team did the right thing.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And I said so in my Facebook post after that; I commended them.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In this case, the facts came out subsequently.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For whatever reasons, they were caught in the wrong place at the wrong time.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Suppose it was an explosive in the trunk of the car, gone through the barricades, crashed into the hotel.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The loss of lives, the loss of reputation, the loss of confidence in our ability.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You want to give our security forces the confidence that when they do their job and when they do it without recklessness or negligence, that the Government Proceedings Act protects them.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is not the place to fully discuss this.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As I have said, if the Member feels strongly, he can put up a Motion.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If you look at the cases that have been prosecuted, they have gone to jail.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It does not give us joy when there is a fatality and our Servicemen go to jail.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Because we know that they were trying to do the job, yet, somewhat enthusiastic.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We send a signal that this is wrong and they get on with their lives after that.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Member says, "Why not lift it from training?" You can train at one place and expect your security forces to ramp up their capabilities when in real operations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There is a saying, "If you don't sweat in training, you will spill blood in real operations." You have to make your training realistic so that when they meet those circumstances – like the guard who fired at the car and stopped the car in time.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Do you think you can get that level of proficiency if they think they are not protected during training?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is something for the House to debate and for Singaporeans to decide.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: To be fair, other countries have done away with it and many of them have regretted it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If the Member feels that other aspects can be looked at, he can raise it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have looked at the facts very carefully.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think we have done right by everyone.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are, of course, sad, but we need still to do what is right for the entire system.
